Winsome

/WIN-sum/ - the stress falls on WIN · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Winsome means charming, pleasing.

The bakery's winsome new apprentice — all freckles, cowlicks, and eager questions — has doubled the number of regulars who stay to chat.

Worked Example

What wins the judges is the young fiddler's winsome stage manner: the bashful bow, the grin at her own wrong note, the little wave to row three.

Winsome charm is innocent and unstudied — it invites affection rather than commanding admiration. A movie star is glamorous; a puppy is winsome. The word leans toward the young, the shy, and the sweet, and it never describes charm that knows its own power.

How Winsome Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

charming

charming: the broad umbrella word for pleasing ways

endearing

endearing: inspiring fondness — winsome's warmest neighbor

Antonyms

grating

grating: charm's opposite — it rubs everyone wrong

off-putting

off-putting: quietly driving people a step back

How Strong Is It? — pleasant → winsome → irresistible

pleasant vs. winsome

pleasant vs. winsome: Pleasant is agreeable, easy company — milder than winsome, which actively draws you in.

irresistible vs. winsome

irresistible vs. winsome: Irresistible goes further than winsome — a winsome smile invites you to smile back; an irresistible one has already decided the matter for you.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of winsome.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — win

Root — win: joy, delight (Old English wynn — not the modern 'win')

Suffix — -some

Suffix — -some: full of, tending to (as in tiresome, quarrelsome)

Put it together

Put it together: Win (joy — Old English wynn) + -some (full of) = full of joy, and therefore joy-giving. The old noun wynn, 'delight,' faded out of English centuries ago, leaving its shape stranded inside this one adjective; the -some ending still builds words freely, from tiresome to quarrelsome. So winsome literally promises what it describes: someone full of delight.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: Old English wynn, 'joy,' survives nowhere else in modern English — winsome is its last address. (The look-alike verb win is a different Old English word, winnan, 'to strive.') The suffix -some, though, is alive and well: handsome, tiresome, quarrelsome.

Strength Check

Word Choice

warm / literary

Winsome praises charm that doesn't know it's charming — childlike, shy, freckled charm. Charming is the all-purpose word; endearing stresses the fondness produced; glamorous is charm with stage lighting. In this unit, winsome describes the person; captivate names what their charm does to the rest of us.
